Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arthur Vance, a 72-year-old retired Chief Petty Officer from the Coast Guard, found himself reliving the night the silence fell. It was decades ago, but for Arthur, the memory was not distant. It played out in his mind like a film, vivid and unbidden, showing him the scene just as if he were looking at photographs of it. He could see the dimly lit corridor of the cutter, the sudden, unnatural cessation of the ship’s usual mechanical hum. That unusual silence had always been the first sign, a premonition that something dangerous was about to happen, far more terrifying than the alarms that followed. Then came the acrid, metallic smell, the burning in his lungs, the frantic scramble to contain the ruptured chemical line in the engine room, the unconscious crewmate he dragged to safety, and the invisible, corrosive mist that stung his eyes and skin.

Now, in the quiet of his retirement, these memories would return with an overwhelming force, leaving him breathless and disoriented. When they played, he would feel so flooded with emotion – the terror, the helplessness, the burning in his chest – that he would have to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes simply sitting frozen in his armchair, waiting for the wave to pass. He had come to believe that if he ever truly allowed himself to think about the event, to delve into the details or the feelings, he would simply not be able to handle it. The potential for emotional collapse felt too great.

This constant internal battle had subtly reshaped his life. The world, he was certain, was a dangerous place, filled with unseen threats, and this conviction made him feel perpetually on guard. Even within the familiar walls of his own home, the place he shared with his wife, Eleanor, he felt an unnerving vigilance. A sudden quiet moment, the hum of the refrigerator cutting out, or the absence of the usual neighborhood sounds, could send a shiver down his spine, his heart rate quickening, his muscles tensing. These were the moments when his body would react with a powerful, involuntary jolt, his breath catching, a wave of physical reactivity washing over him as if he were back on that ship, facing the invisible poison once more.

Over the years, Arthur found himself increasingly fragile. He had come to believe he couldn't deal with even the slightest upset, whether it was a minor disagreement with Eleanor or a frustrating phone call about a bill. He would retreat, avoiding any situation that might trigger an emotional response, fearing he would simply shatter. Eleanor, once his steady companion in daily walks and shared hobbies, found him more withdrawn, his eyes constantly scanning, his responses often clipped or irritable. He stopped joining her for their evening strolls around the block, convinced that something unpredictable might happen, preferring the perceived safety of their living room, though even there, he never truly felt at ease. The joy he once found in his retirement, in quiet mornings and shared meals, was now overshadowed by a persistent, gnawing apprehension, a silent alarm that never truly switched off. It was Eleanor’s gentle but firm insistence, after another night of him pacing the house, unable to sleep, that finally prompted him to seek help, though what frightened him most was the prospect of having to revisit the very memories he had so desperately tried to outrun.
